documents.unit: Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: Syllabus Statements (AI Use statements section)
tiers: No Use of Generative AI Permitted
Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission
Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines
documents.summary: A teaching-center page of optional syllabus statements. Its AI section offers sample wording from other universities in three tiers and tells students to check each class's policy. A separate academic-integrity statement lists unauthorized AI use as misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The AI section says the statements 'help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI, whose use might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline', and offers three sample tiers. The page sets no single rule for all courses, so the stance is delegates with tiers.

units.why: The integrity statement lists 'unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI)' beside cheating and plagiarism, so it classifies AI misuse as academic misconduct. It binds students, applies when misuse occurs, and fits P36 exactly.
units.anchor: unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI)
units.policy: Academic misconduct includes unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI), alongside cheating, plagiarizing, fabricating false sources and unauthorized recording.

units.why: 'The student will be referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office' sets a procedural step once misconduct (which names unauthorized AI) occurs. P81 fits better than P37 because no concrete penalty is named; the grade effect is left to the instructor.
units.anchor: referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office
units.frag_end: through the Dean of Students Office.
units.policy: A student who engages in academic misconduct, which includes unauthorized AI use, may have their grade impacted at the instructor's discretion and is referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office.

units.why: The AI section says the samples 'help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI', i.e. the institution supplies sample AI syllabus language. That is P110, not P63, since it gives wording rather than learning support.
units.anchor: provided to help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI

units.why: The page says generative AI 'might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline and teaching methods their course uses'. No university rule is set; the decision follows discipline and course, so this is P04 (per instructor/course).
units.anchor: whose use might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline
units.policy: Whether generative AI use is appropriate depends on the academic discipline and the teaching methods of the course.

units.why: The page groups its samples under three named headings, from no use to use under some circumstances to broader use. Named levels of permitted AI use are P05; I anchor the middle heading as the clearest span of the scheme.
units.anchor: Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission
units.frag_end: Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines
units.policy: Sample AI statements are grouped in three tiers: No Use of Generative AI Permitted; Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission; Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines.

units.why: The page tells students to 'Make sure to check the specific policies for each of your classes', making them responsible for finding each course's AI rule. It is P78, not P10, because it is not about asking when unsure.
units.anchor: Make sure to check the specific policies for each of your classes.

units.why: The Bryant sample says 'AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage of work in this class', a blanket ban on AI for all work in the course. That is P01 (default ban) rather than P19, which is about producing submitted work.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage of work in this class.

units.why: The same sample says using these tools 'would be considered academically dishonest and a violation of Bryant's Academic Honesty Policy'. It classifies banned AI use as an integrity violation, which is P36.
units.anchor: your actions would be considered academically dishonest
units.policy: Using AI writing tools in the course is academically dishonest and violates the Academic Honesty Policy.

units.why: The Princeton sample says 'All work submitted in this course must be your own', a rule that students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: All work submitted in this course must be your own

units.why: 'You may not ... make use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software' bans AI writing tools for the course work. P19 fits because the concern is AI composing submitted work; P01 is used for the explicit all-stages ban.
units.anchor: make use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software.

units.why: The Colorado sample says 'you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used', so AI use is built into some activities. That is P79 (AI required in some coursework).
units.anchor: you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used
units.frag_end: part of your evaluation in this course.

units.why: 'You are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content ... that will end up in any student work' discourages AI without forbidding it, so P03.
units.anchor: you are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content
units.frag_end: part of your evaluation in this course.
units.policy: Outside the activities that call for AI, students are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content (text, video, audio, images) that ends up in work that is evaluated.

units.why: 'Any student work submitted using AI tools should clearly indicate what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI' asks for disclosure with the submission (P24); it also asks for marking of the AI part but not by tool or prompt.
units.anchor: indicate what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI

units.why: 'No more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI' caps AI-generated content by percentage, which is P16 (AI output allowed under stated conditions, including percentage caps).
units.anchor: no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI

units.why: 'Please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work' tells students to ask the instructor when unsure about the AI rule, which is P10.
units.anchor: please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work

units.why: 'AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class' sets a permissive default for the course, so P02, with the condition of citation handled in the next unit.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class
units.frag_end: cite when and how you use the tool.

units.why: 'Provided that you cite when and how you use the tool' makes citing AI use a condition of using it. This is disclosure with each submission (P24); 'when and how' goes a little beyond a bare statement.
units.anchor: provided that you cite when and how you use the tool
units.frag_end: cite when and how you use the tool.
units.fit_note: Requires citing both when and how the tool was used, which is more detail than a bare disclosure statement.

units.why: 'You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool' commits the instructor to giving citation examples. It supports citing AI (P25) but names no required elements, so it fits only partly.
units.anchor: You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool
units.frag_end: use of this tool in your writing.
units.fit_note: Instructor supplies citation examples; the passage does not say which elements (tool, prompt, output) a citation must contain.

units.why: The Iowa sample calls using an AI-content generator 'without proper attribution or authorization' 'a form of academic dishonesty'. It classifies unattributed or unauthorized AI use as dishonesty (P36).
units.anchor: without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty
units.policy: Using an AI-content generator (such as ChatGPT) to complete coursework without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty.

units.why: 'Work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original' states that submitted work must be the student's own (P29). It is stated apart from the AI sentence, so it is a separate unit.
units.anchor: work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original

units.why: 'If you are unsure about whether something may be plagiarism or academic dishonesty, please contact your instructor' tells students to ask the instructor when unsure, which is P10.
units.anchor: If you are unsure about whether something may be plagiarism or academic dishonesty

documents.unit: Dean of Students, Student Code of Conduct (Bear Code)
documents.title: University Policies: Student Code of Conduct
documents.summary: A 26-page student conduct code with two AI items. Using AI-generated content the instructor or a University Official has not permitted is academic misconduct, and conduct-sanction outcomes may not be produced with generative AI unless indicated. Everything else is general conduct procedure.
documents.stance_why: The code defines 'Unauthorized use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)' as misconduct for AI content 'not permitted by the instructor or University Official'. AI is therefore banned unless permitted, which is restrict. It does not itself say what is permitted.

units.why: The code lists 'Unauthorized use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)' as a type of academic misconduct next to cheating and plagiarism. It binds students and classes AI misuse as misconduct, which is P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI).
units.policy: Unauthorized use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is academic misconduct.

units.why: The definition covers 'written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data generated by' AI that is 'not permitted by the instructor or University Official'. It sets AI as banned unless an instructor or official permits it, and names the instructor as a decider; it is closest to P04, with the default-restrict logic noted.
units.anchor: AI) tools that are not permitted by the instructor or University
units.policy: The use or attempted use of written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data generated by artificial intelligence (AI) tools that are not permitted by the instructor or University Official is unauthorized.
units.fit_note: Permission comes from the instructor or a University Official, and AI not permitted is misconduct, so it works as a restrict-by-default rule as well as a per-instructor rule.

units.why: 'Students are encouraged to review course syllabi to understand the expectations for each course' sits right after the AI item in the misconduct list, telling students to learn each course's rules. It is P78.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to review course syllabi to understand the expectations
units.frag_end: each course in which they are enrolled.

units.why: Outcomes assigned in a conduct case 'are expected to be original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI' unless otherwise indicated. It bans AI from producing submitted work, here sanction assignments, so P19.
units.anchor: original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI
units.policy: Unless otherwise indicated, Outcomes assigned under the Student Code are expected to be original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI.

notes: Both documents are university-level; no college or computing-unit AI policy was collected. Only AI-specific statements were coded. The generic misconduct, hearing, appeal and outcomes procedures in the Student Code were not coded as units because they do not mention AI, though they govern how AI cases are handled. The CETL sample statements are borrowed from Bryant, Princeton, the Colorado system and Iowa and are offered as options, not UNC rules.
